doc.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013

title: Krivin as champion: the Doris Duke Award and Benny Golson
summary: Reid thanks Krivin, who won the Doris Duke Award, brought Golson to write a concerto, and returned to clarinet in retirement.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: because I feel that it’s important that young people see. And I propelled them. I said, “just because you can play up and down your horn and play a lot of notes, that’s not enough. Never has been.” But Marty Krivin, and we are thankful to him that we got a chance to know he and JoAnn, because they made our whole lives change for the better.
Wow. I’ve been lucky to have a couple of those people too, so, I’m glad you got to speak about him.

Yeah. Because we all have to survive. We all have to — but when you can find someone who really — and I never knew what that word meant — someone who champions you. Someone who really champions you. He was the one that actually, because we were the first to get – William Paterson was the first to get the Doris Duke Award. And we had Benny Golson wrote for the orchestra, and he wrote a concerto for me, and he wrote pieces for himself, and we did a thing at Alice Tully Hall with the William Chamber Orchestra. And Marty was responsible for all of it. Because he read everything, and he saw this thing. And we had everything in place that the perspectives on the grant said you had to have. And we had everything. And he applied for it, and he got it. So I mean he was an amazing man. And he was a great clarinet player. He hadn’t played in a long time and when he retired he got the clarinet out and when they went up to Oneonta you know, he got a piano player and they got together.
